claim: Obesity is associated with neurocognitive dysfunction, including memory deficits.
source: Obesity is associated with neurocognitive dysfunction, including memory deficits.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract supported by the broader literature context.

claim: Memory impairments induced by obesogenic high-fat diet (HFD) intake during the periadolescent period can be reversed by chemogenetic manipulation of the ventral hippocampus (vHPC).
source: In rodent models, we recently reported that memory impairments induced by obesogenic high-fat diet (HFD) intake during the periadolescent period can be reversed by chemogenetic manipulation of the ventral hippocampus (vHPC).
evidence: The authors cite their own recent work as support for this claim.

claim: HFD enhanced activation of both vHPC-NAc and vHPC-mPFC pathways after training.
source: We first demonstrated that HFD enhanced activation of both pathways after training and that our chemogenetic approach was effective in normalizing this activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by c-Fos expression data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Chemogenetic inactivation of the vHPC–NAc pathway rescued HFD-induced deficits in recognition memory but not location memory.
source: Inactivation of the vHPC–NAc pathway rescued HFD-induced deficits in recognition but not location memory.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from object recognition and location memory tasks.

claim: Chemogenetic inactivation of the vHPC–mPFC pathway restored location memory but not recognition memory impairments produced by HFD.
source: Conversely, inactivation of the vHPC–mPFC pathway restored location but not recognition memory impairments produced by HFD.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from object recognition and location memory tasks.

claim: Pathway manipulation did not affect exploration or anxiety-like behaviour.
source: Either pathway manipulation did not affect exploration or anxiety-like behaviour.
evidence: This is supported by elevated plus-maze data.

claim: HFD intake throughout adolescence impairs different types of memory through overactivation of specific hippocampal efferent pathways.
source: These findings suggest that HFD intake throughout adolescence impairs different types of memory through overactivation of specific hippocampal efferent pathways and that targeting these overactive pathways has therapeutic potential.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Targeting overactive hippocampal efferent pathways has therapeutic potential for HFD-induced memory deficits.
source: These findings suggest that HFD intake throughout adolescence impairs different types of memory through overactivation of specific hippocampal efferent pathways and that targeting these overactive pathways has therapeutic potential.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: Memory deficits have been previously reported in obese adults.
source: In particular, memory deficits have been previously reported in obese adults (Francis and Stevenson, 2013; Martin and Davidson, 2014; Sellbom and Gunstad, 2012; Yeomans, 2017), but also in obese adolescents (Khan et al., 2015; Nyaradi et al., 2014; Øverby et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Memory deficits have been previously reported in obese adolescents.
source: In particular, memory deficits have been previously reported in obese adults (Francis and Stevenson, 2013; Martin and Davidson, 2014; Sellbom and Gunstad, 2012; Yeomans, 2017), but also in obese adolescents (Khan et al., 2015; Nyaradi et al., 2014; Øverby et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Adolescence is a crucial period for brain development.
source: This is worrisome because the prevalence of obesity during adolescence, a crucial period for brain development (Andersen, 2003; Spear, 2000), has drastically risen (Ogden et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The prevalence of obesity during adolescence has drastically risen.
source: This is worrisome because the prevalence of obesity during adolescence, a crucial period for brain development (Andersen, 2003; Spear, 2000), has drastically risen (Ogden et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Adolescence shows higher vulnerability to the effects of obesogenic diet on hippocampal function and HPC-dependent memory compared to adulthood.
source: Using animal models, we and others have extensively demonstrated the higher vulnerability of adolescence to the effects of obesogenic diet on hippocampal (HPC) function and HPC-dependent memory as compared to adulthood (Boitard et al., 2012; Boitard et al., 2014; Del Olmo and Ruiz-Gayo, 2018; Glushchak et al., 2021; Khazen et al., 2019; Morin et al., 2017; Murray and Chen, 2019; Tsan et al., 2021; Valladolid-Acebes et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Discrete neuronal subpopulations and pathways are particularly vulnerable to dietary manipulations.
source: However, increasing evidence suggest that, rather than homogeneously altering neuronal function, discrete neuronal subpopulations and pathways are particularly vulnerable to dietary manipulations (Berland et al., 2020; Ducrocq et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Some effects of adolescent obesity on specific functional circuits have been reported in humans.
source: Accordingly, few studies reported some effects of adolescent obesity on specific functional circuits in humans (Vega-Torres et al., 2018) and animal models (Moreno-Castilla et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Some effects of adolescent obesity on specific functional circuits have been reported in animal models.
source: Accordingly, few studies reported some effects of adolescent obesity on specific functional circuits in humans (Vega-Torres et al., 2018) and animal models (Moreno-Castilla et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Object-based memory is impaired in HFD-exposed animals.
source: We recently showed that object-based memory is impaired in HFD-exposed animals and that silencing of the ventral hippocampus (vHPC) with Designer Receptor Exclusively Activated by Designer Drugs (DREADD) rescued these memory deficits (Naneix et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' prior work.

claim: Silencing of the ventral hippocampus (vHPC) with DREADD rescued object-based memory deficits in HFD-exposed animals.
source: We recently showed that object-based memory is impaired in HFD-exposed animals and that silencing of the ventral hippocampus (vHPC) with Designer Receptor Exclusively Activated by Designer Drugs (DREADD) rescued these memory deficits (Naneix et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' prior work.

claim: vHPC projections onto the nucleus accumbens (NAc) and the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) represent two of the main monosynaptic targets of the vHPC.
source: We focused on vHPC projections onto the nucleus accumbens (NAc) and the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), because they represent two of the main monosynaptic targets of the vHPC (Britt et al., 2012; Cenquizca and Swanson, 2007; Ciocchi et al., 2015; Gergues et al., 2020; Liu and Carter, 2018), they modulate object-based memory (Barker et al., 2017; Nelson et al., 2011; Sargolini et al., 2003) and we and others previously demonstrated that, in addition to the HPC, periadolescent HFD affects both NAc and mPFC functions (Ducrocq et al., 2019; Labouesse et al., 2013; Labouesse et al., 2017; Naneix et al., 2017; Reichelt et al., 2019; Yaseen et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: vHPC projections to NAc and mPFC modulate object-based memory.
source: We focused on vHPC projections onto the nucleus accumbens (NAc) and the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), because they represent two of the main monosynaptic targets of the vHPC (Britt et al., 2012; Cenquizca and Swanson, 2007; Ciocchi et al., 2015; Gergues et al., 2020; Liu and Carter, 2018), they modulate object-based memory (Barker et al., 2017; Nelson et al., 2011; Sargolini et al., 2003) and we and others previously demonstrated that, in addition to the HPC, periadolescent HFD affects both NAc and mPFC functions (Ducrocq et al., 2019; Labouesse et al., 2013; Labouesse et al., 2017; Naneix et al., 2017; Reichelt et al., 2019; Yaseen et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Periadolescent HFD affects both NAc and mPFC functions.
source: We focused on vHPC projections onto the nucleus accumbens (NAc) and the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), because they represent two of the main monosynaptic targets of the vHPC (Britt et al., 2012; Cenquizca and Swanson, 2007; Ciocchi et al., 2015; Gergues et al., 2020; Liu and Carter, 2018), they modulate object-based memory (Barker et al., 2017; Nelson et al., 2011; Sargolini et al., 2003) and we and others previously demonstrated that, in addition to the HPC, periadolescent HFD affects both NAc and mPFC functions (Ducrocq et al., 2019; Labouesse et al., 2013; Labouesse et al., 2017; Naneix et al., 2017; Reichelt et al., 2019; Yaseen et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Both vHPC-NAc and vHPC-mPFC pathways were hyperactive in HFD animals after object-based learning.
source: We found that both pathways were hyperactive in HFD animals after object-based learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by c-Fos expression data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The vHPC sends dense projections to both the NAc and the mPFC.
source: It is well known that the vHPC sends dense projections to both the NAc and the mPFC.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Numerous fibres expressing tdTomato were detected in the NAc after AAV-CaMKII-Cre injection in the vHPC of Ai14(RCL-tdT)-D mice.
source: As shown in Figure 1, numerous fibres expressing tdTomato were detected in the NAc (Figure 1A) and to a lesser extent in the mPFC (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Fibres expressing tdTomato were detected to a lesser extent in the mPFC compared to NAc after AAV-CaMKII-Cre injection in the vHPC of Ai14(RCL-tdT)-D mice.
source: As shown in Figure 1, numerous fibres expressing tdTomato were detected in the NAc (Figure 1A) and to a lesser extent in the mPFC (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: mCherry labelling was detected in the vHPC, particularly in the ventral CA1 and subiculum, following injection in both the NAc and the mPFC.
source: We indeed detected mCherry labelling in the vHPC, particularly in the ventral CA1 and subiculum, following injection in both the NAc and the mPFC (Figure 1E,F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1E, F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, E.

claim: After 8 weeks of diet exposure, mice exposed to HFD had significantly higher body weight compared to CD mice.
source: Four weeks after surgery (e.g. after 12 weeks of diet exposure), we found that diet exposure was efficient to induce obesity syndrome since there was a significant diet effect on both body weight and fat mass [F(1,82) = 9.8, p = 0.0025 and F(1,82) = 30.0, p < 0.0001, respectively; other comparisons: F's < 2, p > 0.1; see Table 1].
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight measurements shown in Table 1 and statistical analysis.

claim: After 8 weeks of diet exposure, mice exposed to HFD had significantly higher fat mass compared to CD mice.
source: Four weeks after surgery (e.g. after 12 weeks of diet exposure), we found that diet exposure was efficient to induce obesity syndrome since there was a significant diet effect on both body weight and fat mass [F(1,82) = 9.8, p = 0.0025 and F(1,82) = 30.0, p < 0.0001, respectively; other comparisons: F's < 2, p > 0.1; see Table 1].
evidence: This claim is supported by fat mass measurements shown in Table 1 and statistical analysis.

claim: CD and HFD groups similarly explored novel objects during training, excluding any behavioural influences on c-Fos expression between groups.
source: CD and HFD groups similarly explored the novel objects excluding any behavioural influences on c-Fos expression between groups (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by object exploration data shown in Table 2.

claim: Exposure to HFD resulted in increased c-Fos expression in CA1–subiculum in Control mice.
source: As shown in Figure 2C, exposure to HFD resulted in an increased c-Fos expression in Control mice as demonstrated by a significant effect of diet [F(1,23) = 6.4, p = 0.019].
evidence: This claim is supported by c-Fos quantification data shown in Figure 2C and statistical analysis.

claim: HFD exposure increases the amount of activated CA1 cells projecting to either the NAc or the mPFC.
source: Importantly, this increase was also evident when the double stained cells, c-Fos+ and mCherry+, are considered [F(1,21) = 4.5, p = 0.001; Figure 2D,E], indicating that HFD exposure increases the amount of activated CA1 cells projecting to either the NAc or the mPFC.
evidence: This claim is supported by double-labeling c-Fos and mCherry data shown in Figure 2D, E and statistical analysis.

claim: Silencing either vHPC->NAc or vHPC–mPFC pathway resulted in an attenuation of c-Fos+ cells in CA1.
source: Indeed, as shown on Figure 2C,D silencing either vHPC->NAc or vHPC–mPFC pathway resulted in an attenuation of c-Fos+ cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by c-Fos quantification data shown in Figure 2C, D.

claim: In vHPC–NAc groups, there was a main effect of diet on c-Fos+ cells in CA1.
source: Separate analyses of vHPC–NAc and vHPC–mPFC groups demonstrated, in addition to a main effect of diet [F(1,25) = 4.0, p = 0.056 and F(1,26) = 5.3, p = 0.029, respectively], a main effect of DREADD [F(1,25) = 3.7, p = 0.06 and F(1,26) = 11.0, p = 0.027; interaction: F < 2.5, p > 0.1; Figure 2C].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of c-Fos data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In vHPC–mPFC groups, there was a main effect of diet on c-Fos+ cells in CA1.
source: Separate analyses of vHPC–NAc and vHPC–mPFC groups demonstrated, in addition to a main effect of diet [F(1,25) = 4.0, p = 0.056 and F(1,26) = 5.3, p = 0.029, respectively], a main effect of DREADD [F(1,25) = 3.7, p = 0.06 and F(1,26) = 11.0, p = 0.027; interaction: F < 2.5, p > 0.1; Figure 2C].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of c-Fos data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In vHPC–NAc groups, there was a main effect of DREADD on c-Fos+ cells in CA1.
source: Separate analyses of vHPC–NAc and vHPC–mPFC groups demonstrated, in addition to a main effect of diet [F(1,25) = 4.0, p = 0.056 and F(1,26) = 5.3, p = 0.029, respectively], a main effect of DREADD [F(1,25) = 3.7, p = 0.06 and F(1,26) = 11.0, p = 0.027; interaction: F < 2.5, p > 0.1; Figure 2C].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of c-Fos data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In vHPC–mPFC groups, there was a main effect of DREADD on c-Fos+ cells in CA1.
source: Separate analyses of vHPC–NAc and vHPC–mPFC groups demonstrated, in addition to a main effect of diet [F(1,25) = 4.0, p = 0.056 and F(1,26) = 5.3, p = 0.029, respectively], a main effect of DREADD [F(1,25) = 3.7, p = 0.06 and F(1,26) = 11.0, p = 0.027; interaction: F < 2.5, p > 0.1; Figure 2C].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of c-Fos data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In vHPC–NAc groups, there was a significant effect of diet on double-stained cells (c-Fos+ and mCherry+).
source: Comparable results were obtained when focusing on the double stained cells in both vHPC–NAc and vHPC–mPFC groups since there was a significant effect of diet [F(1,23) = 9.0, p = 0.0063 and F(1,25) = 12.6, p = 0.0016, respectively] and of DREADD [F(1,23) = 8.0, p = 0.0093 and F(1,25) = 10.3, p = 0.0036; interaction: F(1,23) = 3.6, p = 0.07 and F(1,25) = 1.4, p = 0.26; Figure 2D].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of double-labeling data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In vHPC–mPFC groups, there was a significant effect of diet on double-stained cells (c-Fos+ and mCherry+).
source: Comparable results were obtained when focusing on the double stained cells in both vHPC–NAc and vHPC–mPFC groups since there was a significant effect of diet [F(1,23) = 9.0, p = 0.0063 and F(1,25) = 12.6, p = 0.0016, respectively] and of DREADD [F(1,23) = 8.0, p = 0.0093 and F(1,25) = 10.3, p = 0.0036; interaction: F(1,23) = 3.6, p = 0.07 and F(1,25) = 1.4, p = 0.26; Figure 2D].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of double-labeling data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In vHPC–NAc groups, there was a significant effect of DREADD on double-stained cells (c-Fos+ and mCherry+).
source: Comparable results were obtained when focusing on the double stained cells in both vHPC–NAc and vHPC–mPFC groups since there was a significant effect of diet [F(1,23) = 9.0, p = 0.0063 and F(1,25) = 12.6, p = 0.0016, respectively] and of DREADD [F(1,23) = 8.0, p = 0.0093 and F(1,25) = 10.3, p = 0.0036; interaction: F(1,23) = 3.6, p = 0.07 and F(1,25) = 1.4, p = 0.26; Figure 2D].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of double-labeling data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In vHPC–mPFC groups, there was a significant effect of DREADD on double-stained cells (c-Fos+ and mCherry+).
source: Comparable results were obtained when focusing on the double stained cells in both vHPC–NAc and vHPC–mPFC groups since there was a significant effect of diet [F(1,23) = 9.0, p = 0.0063 and F(1,25) = 12.6, p = 0.0016, respectively] and of DREADD [F(1,23) = 8.0, p = 0.0093 and F(1,25) = 10.3, p = 0.0036; interaction: F(1,23) = 3.6, p = 0.07 and F(1,25) = 1.4, p = 0.26; Figure 2D].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of double-labeling data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: HFD induced an increase of c-Fos+ cells in CA3 region which was not attenuated by silencing either vHPC->NAc or vHPC–mPFC pathway.
source: Indeed, when looking at CA3 region, the results showed that HFD induced an increase of c-Fos+ cells which was not attenuated by silencing either vHPC->NAc or vHPC–mPFC pathway as demonstrated by an effect of diet for either vHPC->NAc or vHPC->mPFC groups [F(1,24) = 15.5, p = 0.0006 and F(1,25) = 10.9, p = 0.0029, respectively] but no effect of DREADD or interaction [F's < 2.1, p > 0.16; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A].
evidence: This claim is supported by c-Fos quantification data in CA3 shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and statistical analysis.

claim: HFD increases c-Fos expression in both the NAc and the mPFC.
source: In addition, the impact of diet and DREADD was not restricted to the ventral part of the hippocampus. We indeed found that HFD increases c-Fos expression in both the NAc and the mPFC as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C [diet effect: F(1,22) = 7.0, p = 0.015 and F(1,24) = 14.9, p = 0.0008, respectively].
evidence: This claim is supported by c-Fos quantification data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C and statistical analysis.

claim: DREADD decreased the amount of c-Fos+ cells in the NAc.
source: Interestingly, DREADD was also found to decrease the amount of c-Fos+ cells in the NAc and to a lesser extent in the mPFC [F(1,22) = 8.6, p = 0.0076 and F(1,24) = 2.6, p = 0.11; interaction F's ≤ 1].
evidence: This claim is supported by c-Fos quantification data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and statistical analysis.

claim: DREADD decreased the amount of c-Fos+ cells in the mPFC to a lesser extent than in NAc.
source: Interestingly, DREADD was also found to decrease the amount of c-Fos+ cells in the NAc and to a lesser extent in the mPFC [F(1,22) = 8.6, p = 0.0076 and F(1,24) = 2.6, p = 0.11; interaction F's ≤ 1].
evidence: This claim is supported by c-Fos quantification data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and statistical analysis.

claim: Silencing either vHPC->NAc or vHPC->mPFC pathway normalized HFD-induced over-activation.
source: Altogether, these results show that (1) HFD enhanced c-Fos expression in the ventral CA1–subiculum and more specifically in NAc- and mPFC-projecting vHPC neurons after object-based training and (2) silencing either vHPC->NAc or vHPC->mPFC pathway normalized HFD-induced over-activation, therefore validating our intersectional approach.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the c-Fos data presented.

claim: HFD exposure induced long-term deficits in ORM.
source: We previously demonstrated that HFD exposure induced long-term deficits in ORM (Naneix et al., 2021) and that these deficits could be restored by chemogenetic silencing of the vHPC during training.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' prior work.

claim: Long-term ORM deficits induced by HFD could be restored by chemogenetic silencing of the vHPC during training.
source: We previously demonstrated that HFD exposure induced long-term deficits in ORM (Naneix et al., 2021) and that these deficits could be restored by chemogenetic silencing of the vHPC during training.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' prior work.

claim: CD Control animals spent more time exploring the new object than the familiar one in the ORM task.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, CD Control animals spent more time exploring the new object than the familiar one, which indicates that our training procedure leads to robust long-term ORM (24 hr).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: HFD animals spent the same amount of time exploring new and familiar objects in the ORM task.
source: Consistent with our previous study, we found that HFD exposure induced a strong memory deficit given that HFD animals spent the same amount of time exploring new and familiar objects.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There was a significant effect of diet on ORM performance in Control animals.
source: Such a pattern of results is supported by statistical analysis given that a two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with diet and pathway as factor leads to a significant effect of diet (F(1,22) = 10.9, p = 0.0032) but no effect of pathway or interaction (F's < 0.1, p > 0.9; see Table 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of ORM data shown in Figure 3A and Table 3.

claim: In vHPC–NAc groups, there was a significant diet × DREADD interaction on ORM performance.
source: Such an analysis performed on vHPC–NAc groups leads to a lack of both diet and DREADD effects [F's < 1, p > 0.3; Figure 3A, left] but, importantly however, there was a significant diet × DREADD interaction [F(1,29) = 10.2, p = 0.01].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of ORM data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: HFD-Gi vHPC-NAc group showed higher preference for the novel object than HFD Control vHPC-NAc group in the ORM task.
source: Post hoc analyses reveal a higher preference for the novel object in HFD-Gi than in the HFD Control (p = 0.027).
evidence: This claim is supported by post hoc statistical analysis of ORM data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CD Control vHPC-NAc group explored preferentially the novel object in the ORM task.
source: Looking at the performance of each group, CD Control group explored preferentially the novel object [one sample t-test against 50%; t(6) = 2.67, p = 0.037].
evidence: This claim is supported by one-sample t-test analysis of ORM data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: HFD Control vHPC-NAc group showed no difference in the exploration of the two objects in the ORM task.
source: In contrast, there was no difference in the exploration of the two objects in HFD Control group [t(5) = 0.73, p = 0.49] but a significant difference in HFD-Gi group [t(11) = 6.65, p < 0.0001] which indicates that inactivation of the vHPC–NAc pathway during training restored HFD-induced ORM deficits.
evidence: This claim is supported by one-sample t-test analysis of ORM data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: HFD-Gi vHPC-NAc group showed a significant difference in exploration between novel and familiar objects in the ORM task.
source: In contrast, there was no difference in the exploration of the two objects in HFD Control group [t(5) = 0.73, p = 0.49] but a significant difference in HFD-Gi group [t(11) = 6.65, p < 0.0001] which indicates that inactivation of the vHPC–NAc pathway during training restored HFD-induced ORM deficits.
evidence: This claim is supported by one-sample t-test analysis of ORM data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Inactivation of the vHPC–NAc pathway during training restored HFD-induced ORM deficits.
source: In contrast, there was no difference in the exploration of the two objects in HFD Control group [t(5) = 0.73, p = 0.49] but a significant difference in HFD-Gi group [t(11) = 6.65, p < 0.0001] which indicates that inactivation of the vHPC–NAc pathway during training restored HFD-induced ORM deficits.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the ORM behavioral data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In vHPC->mPFC groups, there was no significant diet × DREADD interaction on ORM performance.
source: Similar analysis performed on the vHPC->mPFC pathway yielded to a different pattern of results. Indeed, a two-way ANOVA with diet and DREADD as factors results in an absence of both diet and DREADD effect but more importantly to a lack of diet x DREADD interaction (All F's < 1.5, p > 0.2; Figure 3A,right).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of ORM data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CD Control vHPC-mPFC group showed ORM performance significantly different from chance.
source: Additional analyses looking at the performance of each group show that ORM was apparent in the CD Control group [t(7) = 7.3, p = 0.0003] but not in the others (t < 1.6, p > 0.14).
evidence: This claim is supported by one-sample t-test analysis of ORM data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Chemogenetic silencing of vHPC->NAc pathway but not of vHPC->mPFC pathway rescued the ORM impairment due to periadolescent HFD diet exposure.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate an important functional dissociation since chemogenetic silencing of vHPC->NAc pathway but not of vHPC->mPFC pathway was shown to rescue the ORM impairment due to periadolescent HFD diet exposure.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the ORM behavioral data.

claim: Periadolescent HFD impairs OLM.
source: We next evaluated the effect of specifically silencing the vHPC pathways on another object-based memory task, the OLM, known to be impaired by periadolescent HFD (Glushchak et al., 2021; Khazen et al., 2019; Valladolid-Acebes et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: CD Control animals spent more time exploring the displaced object than the one left in the same location in the OLM task.
source: As shown in Figure 3B, CD Control animals spent more time exploring the displaced object than the one left in the same location, which indicates that our training procedure leads to robust memory of the object location.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: HFD animals spent the same amount of time exploring the two objects in the OLM task.
source: Consistent with published reports, our results show that that HFD exposure induced a strong OLM deficit given that HFD animals spent the same amount of time exploring the two objects.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There was a significant effect of diet on OLM performance in Control animals.
source: Such conclusions are supported by statistical analysis on control (no DREADD) animals which show a significant effect of diet [F(1,22) = 11.5, p = 0.0026] but no effect of pathway or diet × pathway interaction [F's < 1.3, p > 0.26; Figure 3B; Table 4].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of OLM data shown in Figure 3B and Table 4.

claim: Silencing of vHPC->mPFC, but not vHPC->NAc, pathway restored HFD-induced OLM deficits.
source: Silencing of vHPC->NAc or vHPC->mPFC pathway has a differential impact on the deficits in OLM resulting from HFD exposure, given that silencing of vHPC->NAc has no impact whereas silencing of vHPC->mPFC was efficient in restoring near to normal memory performance.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the OLM behavioral data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In vHPC–mPFC groups, there was a significant diet × DREADD interaction on OLM performance.
source: Indeed, there was a significant diet × DREADD interaction when vHPC–mPFC pathway was manipulated [F(1,28) = 4.3, p = 0.047; diet effect: F(1,28) = 1.9, p = 0.17; DREADD effect: F(1,28) = 13.6, p = 0.001; Figure 3B, right] but not when vHPC–NAc pathway was silenced [F(1,29) = 0.9, p = 0.34; diet effect: F(1,29) = 7.6, p = 0.01; DREADD effect: F(1,29) = 3.0, p = 0.09; Figure 3B, left].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of OLM data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In vHPC–NAc groups, there was no significant diet × DREADD interaction on OLM performance.
source: Indeed, there was a significant diet × DREADD interaction when vHPC–mPFC pathway was manipulated [F(1,28) = 4.3, p = 0.047; diet effect: F(1,28) = 1.9, p = 0.17; DREADD effect: F(1,28) = 13.6, p = 0.001; Figure 3B, right] but not when vHPC–NAc pathway was silenced [F(1,29) = 0.9, p = 0.34; diet effect: F(1,29) = 7.6, p = 0.01; DREADD effect: F(1,29) = 3.0, p = 0.09; Figure 3B, left].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of OLM data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: HFD Gi vHPC–mPFC group showed significantly higher preference for the displaced object than HFD Control vHPC–mPFC group in the OLM task.
source: Post hoc analyses indicated a significantly higher preference for the displaced object in HFD Gi vHPC–mPFC group than in HFD Control vHPC–mPFC group (p = 0.0017).
evidence: This claim is supported by post hoc statistical analysis of OLM data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: CD-fed Control mice explored preferentially the displaced object in the OLM task.
source: Looking at the performance of each group, CD-fed Control mice explored preferentially the displaced object [one sample t-test against 50%: vHPC–NAc: t(6) = 2.97, p = 0.025; vHPC–mPFC: t(6) = 3.36, p = 0.015] whereas HFD Control groups exhibited OLM deficits, exploring both objects similarly [vHPC–NAc: t(5) = 0.12, p = 0.91; vHPC–mPFC: t(5) = 0.49, p = 0.64; Figure 3B].
evidence: This claim is supported by one-sample t-test analysis of OLM data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: HFD Control groups exhibited OLM deficits, exploring both objects similarly.
source: Looking at the performance of each group, CD-fed Control mice explored preferentially the displaced object [one sample t-test against 50%: vHPC–NAc: t(6) = 2.97, p = 0.025; vHPC–mPFC: t(6) = 3.36, p = 0.015] whereas HFD Control groups exhibited OLM deficits, exploring both objects similarly [vHPC–NAc: t(5) = 0.12, p = 0.91; vHPC–mPFC: t(5) = 0.49, p = 0.64; Figure 3B].
evidence: This claim is supported by one-sample t-test analysis of OLM data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Chemogenetic silencing of the vHPC–NAc pathway before training had no effect on OLM performance in HFD-fed mice.
source: In HFD-fed mice, chemogenetic silencing of the vHPC–NAc pathway before training had no effect on OLM performance [t(11) = 0.9, p = 0.40], whereas manipulation of the vHPC–mPFC pathway improved it [t(10) = 5.4, p = 0.0003].
evidence: This claim is supported by one-sample t-test analysis of OLM data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Manipulation of the vHPC–mPFC pathway improved OLM performance in HFD-fed mice.
source: In HFD-fed mice, chemogenetic silencing of the vHPC–NAc pathway before training had no effect on OLM performance [t(11) = 0.9, p = 0.40], whereas manipulation of the vHPC–mPFC pathway improved it [t(10) = 5.4, p = 0.0003].
evidence: This claim is supported by one-sample t-test analysis of OLM data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Chemogenetic silencing of the vHPC–NAc pathway before training impaired OLM performance in CD-fed mice.
source: In CD-fed mice, chemogenetic silencing of the vHPC–NAc pathway before training impaired OLM performance [t(7) = 1.0, p = 0.33] whereas manipulation of the vHPC–mPFC pathway had no effect [t(7) = 5.7, p = 0.0007].
evidence: This claim is supported by one-sample t-test analysis of OLM data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Manipulation of the vHPC–mPFC pathway had no effect on OLM performance in CD-fed mice.
source: In CD-fed mice, chemogenetic silencing of the vHPC–NAc pathway before training impaired OLM performance [t(7) = 1.0, p = 0.33] whereas manipulation of the vHPC–mPFC pathway had no effect [t(7) = 5.7, p = 0.0007].
evidence: This claim is supported by one-sample t-test analysis of OLM data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Adult HFD intake has been reported to affect anxiety-like behaviour.
source: Adult HFD intake (Fulton et al., 2022) or manipulation of specific vHPC pathways (Padilla-Coreano et al., 2016; Parfitt et al., 2017) has been reported to affect anxiety-like behaviour.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Manipulation of specific vHPC pathways has been reported to affect anxiety-like behaviour.
source: Adult HFD intake (Fulton et al., 2022) or manipulation of specific vHPC pathways (Padilla-Coreano et al., 2016; Parfitt et al., 2017) has been reported to affect anxiety-like behaviour.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: There was no effect of HFD or vHPC pathway inhibition on the percentage of time spent in open arm in the Elevated-Plus Maze test.
source: There was no effect of HFD or vHPC pathway inhibition on the percentage of time spent in open arm [diet × pathway: F(1,17) = 0.7, p = 0.41; diet × DREADD: F(1,25) = 1.1, p = 0.29 for vHPC–NAc groups, F(1,24) = 0.6, p = 0.44 for vHPC–mPFC groups; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B] or the percentage of open arm entries [diet × pathway: F(1,17) = 0.2, p = 0.69; diet × DREADD: F(1,25) = 0.01, p = 0.92 for vHPC–NAc groups, F(1,24) = 0.18, p = 0.68 for vHPC–mPFC groups; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of EPM data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There was no effect of HFD or vHPC pathway inhibition on the percentage of open arm entries in the Elevated-Plus Maze test.
source: There was no effect of HFD or vHPC pathway inhibition on the percentage of time spent in open arm [diet × pathway: F(1,17) = 0.7, p = 0.41; diet × DREADD: F(1,25) = 1.1, p = 0.29 for vHPC–NAc groups, F(1,24) = 0.6, p = 0.44 for vHPC–mPFC groups; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B] or the percentage of open arm entries [diet × pathway: F(1,17) = 0.2, p = 0.69; diet × DREADD: F(1,25) = 0.01, p = 0.92 for vHPC–NAc groups, F(1,24) = 0.18, p = 0.68 for vHPC–mPFC groups; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of EPM data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Neither periadolescent HFD nor vHPC pathway manipulation affect anxiety-like behaviour.
source: These results indicate that neither periadolescent HFD nor vHPC pathway manipulation affect anxiety-like behaviour, and therefore exclude that any effects on memory performance would be due to differences in anxiety levels among the groups.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the EPM data.

claim: Periadolescent HFD-induced deficits in non-aversive and non-rewarded object-based memory in mice, without affecting anxiety-like behaviour.
source: The current study provides evidence that periadolescent HFD-induced deficits in non-aversive and non-rewarded object-based memory in mice, without affecting anxiety-like behaviour.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: Memory deficits induced by periadolescent HFD were associated with enhanced activation of vHPC neurons projecting to NAc and mPFC.
source: These memory deficits were associated with enhanced activation of vHPC neurons projecting to NAc and mPFC.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the c-Fos findings.

claim: The pathway-specific chemogenetic approach was effective in normalizing the enhanced activation of vHPC neurons projecting to NAc and mPFC.
source: Using a pathway-specific chemogenetic approach that was effective in normalizing this activation, we demonstrated that (1) silencing of NAc-projecting, but not mPFC-projecting, vHPC neurons restored long-term ORM deficits induced by HFD whereas (2) inactivation of mPFC-projecting, but not NAc-projecting, vHPC neurons rescued HFD-induced OLM deficits.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the chemogenetic manipulation findings.

claim: Silencing of NAc-projecting, but not mPFC-projecting, vHPC neurons restored long-term ORM deficits induced by HFD.
source: Using a pathway-specific chemogenetic approach that was effective in normalizing this activation, we demonstrated that (1) silencing of NAc-projecting, but not mPFC-projecting, vHPC neurons restored long-term ORM deficits induced by HFD whereas (2) inactivation of mPFC-projecting, but not NAc-projecting, vHPC neurons rescued HFD-induced OLM deficits.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the ORM findings.

claim: Inactivation of mPFC-projecting, but not NAc-projecting, vHPC neurons rescued HFD-induced OLM deficits.
source: Using a pathway-specific chemogenetic approach that was effective in normalizing this activation, we demonstrated that (1) silencing of NAc-projecting, but not mPFC-projecting, vHPC neurons restored long-term ORM deficits induced by HFD whereas (2) inactivation of mPFC-projecting, but not NAc-projecting, vHPC neurons rescued HFD-induced OLM deficits.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the OLM findings.

claim: The results revealed a double dissociation in the beneficial outcomes of vHPC–NAc or vHPC–mPFC silencing on HFD-induced ORM and OLM deficits.
source: Our results therefore revealed a double dissociation in the beneficial outcomes of vHPC–NAc or vHPC–mPFC silencing on HFD-induced ORM and OLM deficits, without any effect on anxiety-like behaviour.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the behavioral findings.

claim: 12 weeks of periadolescent HFD induced a higher c-Fos activation of the dorsal hippocampus after object-based training.
source: Our previous studies revealed that 12 weeks of periadolescent HFD induced a higher c-Fos activation of the dorsal hippocampus after object-based training (Biyong et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' prior work.

claim: A large neural network including vHPC, NAc shell, and mPFC is overactive in HFD-fed mice following object training.
source: Here, we obtained similar c-Fos overexpression in the CA1/subiculum of the vHPC after object training, as well as in projecting areas NAc shell and mPFC, providing evidence that a large neural network is overactive in HFD-fed mice following object training.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the c-Fos data presented in the manuscript.

claim: HFD effect on c-Fos expression is more pronounced in ventral CA1 and subiculum, which represent the main output of the vHPC.
source: In HPC, HFD effect is more pronounced in ventral CA1 and subiculum, which represent the main output of the vHPC (Britt et al., 2012; Cenquizca and Swanson, 2007; Ciocchi et al., 2015; Gergues et al., 2020; Liu and Carter, 2018).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the c-Fos data combined with anatomical knowledge from cited literature.

claim: 8–12 weeks of post-weaning HFD intake enhances dendritic spine density in CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: This could be related to HFD-induced morphological and electrophysiological changes in CA1 as it was reported that 8–12 weeks of post-weaning HFD intake enhances dendritic spine density in CA1 pyramidal neurons (Valladolid-Acebes et al., 2013) and induces aberrant in vivo long-term potentiation in CA1 (Vouimba et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: 8–12 weeks of post-weaning HFD intake induces aberrant in vivo long-term potentiation in CA1.
source: This could be related to HFD-induced morphological and electrophysiological changes in CA1 as it was reported that 8–12 weeks of post-weaning HFD intake enhances dendritic spine density in CA1 pyramidal neurons (Valladolid-Acebes et al., 2013) and induces aberrant in vivo long-term potentiation in CA1 (Vouimba et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: CNO decreased the activation of vHPC-to-NAc and vHPC-to-mPFC neurons expressing inhibitory DREADDs in HFD-fed mice.
source: Importantly, Clozapine-N-Oxide (CNO) decreased the activation of vHPC-to-NAc and vHPC-to-mPFC neurons expressing inhibitory DREADDs in HFD-fed mice, validating the efficacy of our intersectional chemogenetic approach.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the c-Fos data validating the chemogenetic approach.

claim: Restricted chemogenetic inhibition tends to attenuate HFD-induced overactivation of the whole ventral CA1/subiculum, possibly through a network effect.
source: This restricted chemogenetic inhibition tends to attenuate HFD-induced overactivation of the whole ventral CA1/subiculum, possibly through a network effect.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the c-Fos data.

claim: Periadolescent HFD induces long-term ORM deficits.
source: Our results indicate that periadolescent HFD induces long-term ORM deficits, corroborating our recent studies showing specific HFD effects on long-term, but not short-term, ORM (Biyong et al., 2021; Naneix et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by the current data and citations to the authors' prior work.

claim: HFD has specific effects on long-term, but not short-term, ORM.
source: Our results indicate that periadolescent HFD induces long-term ORM deficits, corroborating our recent studies showing specific HFD effects on long-term, but not short-term, ORM (Biyong et al., 2021; Naneix et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the authors' prior work.

claim: Chemogenetic inactivation of vHPC projecting neurons during training, by restricting DREADDs expression primarily to excitatory principal neurons, is able to restore HFD-induced ORM deficits.
source: We had previously reported that chemogenetic inactivation of vHPC projecting neurons during training, by restricting DREADDs expression primarily to excitatory principal neurons thanks to the use of a CaMKII promoter, is able to restore HFD-induced ORM deficits (Naneix et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' prior work.

claim: HFD affects NAc functions after periadolescent HFD exposure.
source: This finding supports previous results indicating that HFD affects NAc functions after periadolescent HFD exposure (Ducrocq et al., 2019; Labouesse et al., 2013; Naneix et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Silencing NAc-projecting vHPC neurons attenuated ORM in controls.
source: Moreover, silencing NAc-projecting vHPC neurons attenuated ORM in controls in line with previous findings demonstrating the role of NAc in ORM consolidation (Sargolini et al., 2003) and in integrating HPC-derived information during memory consolidation (Kerfoot and Williams, 2018; Roozendaal et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by the current data and citations to prior literature.

claim: NAc plays a role in ORM consolidation.
source: Moreover, silencing NAc-projecting vHPC neurons attenuated ORM in controls in line with previous findings demonstrating the role of NAc in ORM consolidation (Sargolini et al., 2003) and in integrating HPC-derived information during memory consolidation (Kerfoot and Williams, 2018; Roozendaal et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NAc plays a role in integrating HPC-derived information during memory consolidation.
source: Moreover, silencing NAc-projecting vHPC neurons attenuated ORM in controls in line with previous findings demonstrating the role of NAc in ORM consolidation (Sargolini et al., 2003) and in integrating HPC-derived information during memory consolidation (Kerfoot and Williams, 2018; Roozendaal et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Periadolescent exposure to HFD drastically affects spatial memory assessed in the Morris water maze or the radial arm maze.
source: Previous findings indicate that periadolescent exposure to HFD drastically affects spatial memory assessed in the Morris water maze or the radial arm maze (Boitard et al., 2012; Boitard et al., 2014) but also using non-aversive and non-rewarded OLM (Glushchak et al., 2021; Khazen et al., 2019; Valladolid-Acebes et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Periadolescent HFD alters mPFC functions.
source: Our results are related to previous studies indicating that periadolescent HFD alters mPFC functions (Labouesse et al., 2017; Reichelt et al., 2019; Yaseen et al., 2019) and that vHPC–mPFC pathway modulates different aspects of object-based memory (Barker et al., 2017; Morici et al., 2022; Nelson et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: vHPC–mPFC pathway modulates different aspects of object-based memory.
source: Our results are related to previous studies indicating that periadolescent HFD alters mPFC functions (Labouesse et al., 2017; Reichelt et al., 2019; Yaseen et al., 2019) and that vHPC–mPFC pathway modulates different aspects of object-based memory (Barker et al., 2017; Morici et al., 2022; Nelson et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: CNO action lasts several hours.
source: As CNO action lasts several hours (Alexander et al., 2009), mPFC–vHPC pathways were inactivated during both OLM training and test.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: mPFC–vHPC pathways were inactivated during both OLM training and test.
source: As CNO action lasts several hours (Alexander et al., 2009), mPFC–vHPC pathways were inactivated during both OLM training and test.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of CNO administration and its duration of action.

claim: A very small proportion (5–10%) of vHPC neurons project to two or three areas.
source: Recent studies indicate that a very small proportion (5–10%) of vHPC neurons project to two or three areas (Ciocchi et al., 2015; Gergues et al., 2020; Parfitt et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The double dissociation in effects of pathway-specific silencing on ORM and OLM precludes that collaterals of mPFC- and NAc-projecting vHPC neurons may be involved in the effects.
source: However, the double dissociation in our effects of pathway-specific silencing on ORM and OLM precludes that collaterals of mPFC- and NAc-projecting vHPC neurons may be involved in our effects.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the pattern of results.

claim: The dissociation observed in the present study excludes any influences of sensory, motor, motivational or attentional processes on the memory effects.
source: Also, this dissociation observed in the present study excludes any influences of sensory, motor, motivational or attentional processes, which would have similarly affected both memory tasks.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the specificity of the effects.

claim: Diet or pathway manipulation did not affect anxiety-like behaviour, ruling out that effects on memory were due to differences in anxiety levels among the groups.
source: Finally, our diet or pathway manipulation did not affect anxiety-like behaviour, ruling out that our effects on memory were due to differences in anxiety levels among the groups.

claim: Juvenile or periadolescent HFD exposure does not affect anxiety-like behaviour.
source: This is in line with previous studies performed after juvenile or periadolescent HFD exposure (André et al., 2014; Boitard et al., 2015; Hayes et al., 2023; Khazen et al., 2019; Tsan et al., 2022) but in contrast with others showing that adult HFD exposure triggered anxiety-like behaviour (Décarie-Spain et al., 2018; Fulton et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Adult HFD exposure triggered anxiety-like behaviour.
source: This is in line with previous studies performed after juvenile or periadolescent HFD exposure (André et al., 2014; Boitard et al., 2015; Hayes et al., 2023; Khazen et al., 2019; Tsan et al., 2022) but in contrast with others showing that adult HFD exposure triggered anxiety-like behaviour (Décarie-Spain et al., 2018; Fulton et al., 2022).

source: The current study provides evidence that periadolescent HFD induces deficits in different types of memory through an over-activation of specific vHPC efferent pathways and dampening this activation alleviates these memory deficits.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the main findings.

claim: Dampening the over-activation of specific vHPC efferent pathways alleviates memory deficits induced by periadolescent HFD.
source: The current study provides evidence that periadolescent HFD induces deficits in different types of memory through an over-activation of specific vHPC efferent pathways and dampening this activation alleviates these memory deficits.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the main findings.

claim: The findings extend knowledge about the cerebral impact of obesogenic diet focusing on brain network and connectivity.
source: These findings extend our knowledge about the cerebral impact of obesogenic diet focusing on brain network and connectivity and emphasize the distinct role of specific vHPC efferent pathways in different types of object-based memory.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the significance of the findings.

source: Future studies are required to examine the effects of manipulation of vHPC pathways, including those to anterior olfactory nucleus (Aqrabawi and Kim, 2018), in other types of memory impairments promoted by HFD, such as social and olfactory memory (Reichelt et al., 2019; Yaseen et al., 2019).

claim: HFD impairs social and olfactory memory.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions.

claim: HPC hyperactivity plays an important role in memory decline associated with normal and pathological ageing.
source: According to the important role played by HPC hyperactivity in memory decline associated with normal and pathological ageing (Bakker et al., 2012; Yassa et al., 2011) as well as disruption of vHPC efferent pathways in neuropsychiatric disorders (Bagot et al., 2015; Li et al., 2015; Phillips et al., 2019), future research has to contribute to the development of novel therapeutic strategies to alleviate disorders characterised by impaired HPC homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

source: According to the important role played by HPC hyperactivity in memory decline associated with normal and pathological ageing (Bakker et al., 2012; Yassa et al., 2011) as well as disruption of vHPC efferent pathways in neuropsychiatric disorders (Bagot et al., 2015; Li et al., 2015; Phillips et al., 2019), future research has to contribute to the development of novel therapeutic strategies to alleviate disorders characterised by impaired HPC homeostasis.

claim: Male C57BL/6J mice were used in the study.
source: Male C57BL/6J mice aged of 3 weeks old (Janvier Labs, France) were divided randomly into groups of 8 per cage (45 × 25 × 20 cm, containing a paper house, nesting material and a small wooden stick) and had ad libitum access to a control diet (CD; n = 43; 2.9 kcal/g; 8% lipids, 19% proteins, 73% carbohydrates mostly from starch; A04, SAFE) or a HFD (n = 64; 4.7 kcal/g; 45% lipids mostly saturated fat from lard, 20% proteins, 35% carbohydrates mainly from sucrose; D12451, Research Diet).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: The study focused on males because female rodents do not consistently exhibit memory deficits after post-weaning obesogenic diet intake.
source: We focused on males given that female rodents do not consistently exhibit memory deficits after post-weaning obesogenic diet intake (see Abbott et al., 2016; Hwang et al., 2010), which is probably related to ovarian hormones that appear to protect females from obesity and metabolic impairments (Palmer and Clegg, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Ovarian hormones appear to protect females from obesity and metabolic impairments.

evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Animals were housed in a temperature-controlled room (22 ± 1°C) maintained under a 12-hr light/dark cycle.
source: All animals were housed in a temperature-controlled room (22 ± 1°C) maintained under a 12-hr light/dark cycle (lights on at 8:00 am, lights off at 8:00 pm) and had free access to food and water during 12 weeks (before the beginning of behaviour) as well as during all behavioural procedures before euthanasia (13–14 weeks of diet exposure in total).
evidence: This is a description of the housing conditions.
